title: What ṣarf is, and why it comes first
summary: Ṣarf is the science of the single word: its root, its pattern and the forms a root takes. In the madrasa it is read before naḥw.

sections.heading: The science of the word
paragraphs: Ṣarf, also called taṣrīf, looks at a word on its own. It weighs every word against the scale فَعَلَ, sorts verbs into bare and augmented patterns, conjugates them through the fourteen persons, and derives from one root the verbal noun, the active and passive participles and the other nouns.
It also explains the changes that weak letters undergo, iʿlāl, which turn the root q-w-l into قَالَ and يَقُولُ. A student who knows these rules can find any word in a dictionary arranged by roots.

sections.heading: Why it comes first
paragraphs: Naḥw judges the ending of a word, but it can only do so once the word itself is recognised: whether يُكْرَمُ is a verb, which person, active or passive. That is why the Indian and Ottoman madrasas begin with ṣarf, and why a saying of the teachers calls ṣarf the mother of the sciences and naḥw their father.

Its classic first books differ by region: Mīzān al-ṣarf and Ṣarf-i Mīr in Persian in India, al-Amthila and Bināʾ al-afʿāl in the Ottoman lands, al-Taṣrīf al-ʿIzzī and Lāmiyyat al-afʿāl in the Arab world.
